marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q001.takeaway: RAS stimulation produces an EEG alerting response and wakes the animal.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q001.displayText: The reticular activating system (RAS/ARAS) is a polysynaptic brainstem–hypothalamic network receiving sensory collaterals and projecting through intralaminar/reticular thalamic nuclei diffusely to cortex. High-frequency midbrain reticular stimulation produces EEG desynchronization/alerting and arousal; therefore the false statement is that it does not produce an alerting response.

rationales.a: Arousal is a core function of the reticular activating system.
rationales.b: RAS is a polysynaptic brainstem/hypothalamic pathway with diffuse thalamocortical projections.
rationales.c: Ascending sensory tracts and special-sense pathways send collaterals into the RAS.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q002.takeaway: Relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed produces alpha waves.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q002.displayText: Alpha activity is prominent over parieto-occipital scalp in a relaxed, awake adult with eyes closed. Opening the eyes or concentrating suppresses alpha and increases faster beta activity; theta and delta predominate in drowsiness/deeper sleep.

rationales.b: Beta activity is more associated with alert attention and active mental processing than relaxed eyes-closed rest.
rationales.c: Theta is associated with drowsiness/light sleep rather than the awake relaxed state.
rationales.d: Delta is characteristic of deep NREM slow-wave sleep, not quiet wakefulness.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q003.takeaway: Hypothalamic centers and the ascending reticular system regulate the sleep–wake cycle.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q003.displayText: The hypothalamus and midbrain ascending reticular activating system regulate sleep–wake transitions. Locus coeruleus norepinephrine and raphe serotonin support arousal; pontine cholinergic neurons promote sleep/REM transitions, anterior hypothalamus and basal forebrain promote NREM sleep through GABAergic neurons, and posterior hypothalamic histamine supports wakefulness. Orexin stabilizes transitions.

rationales.a: Basal ganglia participate in motor and habit circuits; they are not the primary sleep–wake regulators.
rationales.c: Medullary autonomic and respiratory functions are distinct from the hypothalamic/ARAS sleep-wake network.
rationales.d: Cerebellum coordinates movement; it does not set the principal sleep–wake cycle.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q004.takeaway: K complexes and sleep spindles identify NREM stage 2.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q004.displayText: Stage N2 is marked by 12–14 Hz sleep spindles and occasional high-voltage biphasic K complexes. Their appearance distinguishes N2 from N1, while N3 is dominated by high-amplitude delta activity and REM has activated mixed-frequency EEG with rapid eye movements.

rationales.a: REM sleep has mixed, activated EEG and rapid eye movements, not the characteristic N2 spindle/K-complex pair.
rationales.b: N1 is the transition into sleep; spindles and K complexes emerge in N2.
rationales.d: N3 is slow-wave sleep dominated by delta waves.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q005.takeaway: NREM stage 2 accounts for the greatest share of young-adult sleep.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q005.displayText: Young adults spend the largest share of sleep in N2, about 50–60% in the source estimate. REM occupies roughly 20–25%, N3 about 15–20%, and N1 around 5%; the percentages shift across development and age, with much more REM in infants.

rationales.a: REM is a substantial but smaller share of young-adult sleep than N2.
rationales.b: N1 is a brief transition stage and accounts for only about 5% in the source estimate.
rationales.d: N3 contributes around 15–20%, less than N2.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q006.takeaway: Increased acetylcholine activity in pontine reticular neurons is associated with sleep induction.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q006.displayText: Pontine cholinergic activity promotes sleep induction in the source model. Wakefulness is associated with active locus-coeruleus norepinephrine and raphe serotonin systems; a shift toward pontine acetylcholine and sleep-promoting hypothalamic/basal-forebrain GABA activity supports sleep and REM transitions.

rationales.a: Norepinephrine and serotonin activity is associated with arousal in this source model, not increased sleep induction.
rationales.c: Histamine neurons in posterior hypothalamus promote arousal rather than sleep onset.
rationales.d: GABAergic inhibition promotes NREM sleep; sleep induction is not associated with decreased GABA.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q007.takeaway: Dorsal raphe serotonergic neurons promote arousal and are not the NREM sleep-promoting site asked for.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q007.displayText: The dorsal raphe contains serotonergic neurons that contribute to arousal; in this source’s sleep-state distinction, it is not part of the NREM sleep-promoting network. Anterior hypothalamic and basal-forebrain GABAergic neurons promote NREM sleep, while thalamocortical rhythmic activity produces synchronized slow EEG waves.

rationales.b: Thalamocortical relay activity generates synchronized cortical potentials in NREM sleep.
rationales.c: Anterior hypothalamus is a sleep-promoting region in the source account.
rationales.d: Basal forebrain GABAergic NREM-on neurons help induce sleep.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q008.takeaway: Delta waves are characteristic of deep, slow-wave sleep.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q008.displayText: Delta waves dominate N3 slow-wave sleep, historically stages 3 and 4. They reflect synchronized thalamocortical activity during deep NREM rather than the activated EEG of REM or relaxed wakefulness.

rationales.b: REM EEG is activated/mixed-frequency rather than predominantly delta.
rationales.c: Awake relaxed adults show alpha, while alert attention increases beta activity.
rationales.d: N1 is light transitional sleep; delta predominates in N3.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q010.takeaway: Pinealocytes in the pineal gland secrete melatonin.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q010.displayText: Pinealocytes in the pineal gland synthesize and release melatonin, a signal involved in sleep timing. The pineal gland is prominent in infancy and undergoes age-related involution and calcification; melatonin secretion rises in darkness and falls in daylight.

rationales.b: The hypothalamus regulates circadian timing but is not the organ that secretes melatonin.
rationales.c: Adrenal cortex produces steroid hormones, not melatonin.
rationales.d: Melanocytes synthesize skin pigment; melatonin is produced by pinealocytes.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q011.takeaway: Melatonin helps regulate circadian timing and sleep–wake rhythm.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q011.displayText: Melatonin provides a timing cue for circadian rhythms and can help resynchronize sleep–wake timing after jet lag. Its synthesis and secretion rise during darkness and remain low in daylight; it promotes sleepiness rather than releasing melanin or directly facilitating ACTH secretion.

rationales.a: ACTH timing is governed by hypothalamic-pituitary signals and the SCN rhythm; melatonin’s keyed role is circadian coordination.
rationales.b: Melatonin supports sleepiness and timing; it does not prevent sleep induction.
rationales.d: Melanin is a pigment; melatonin is a pineal hormone with circadian effects.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q012.takeaway: Basal ganglia participate in procedural memory for skills and habits.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q012.displayText: Procedural (implicit) memory stores skills and habits that become automatic and is associated with striatal circuitry. Declarative memory is conscious recall of facts and events and depends on medial temporal structures, hippocampus, and neocortex; priming and conditioning are other forms of implicit learning.

rationales.a: Conditioning is associative learning involving amygdala (emotional) or cerebellum (motor) circuits rather than the basal-ganglia skill/habit category asked here.
rationales.c: Explicit memory involves conscious facts/events and medial temporal structures, not the basal-ganglia procedural loop.
rationales.d: Basal ganglia do contribute to implicit procedural memory, so ‘none’ is incorrect.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q013.takeaway: Mammillary-body injury can disrupt consolidation and cause anterograde amnesia.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q013.displayText: The mammillary bodies, hippocampus, and mammillothalamic tract participate in converting short-term memories into durable long-term memories. Compression or injury to the mammillary body can impair new-memory formation and cause anterograde amnesia, as in lesions affecting this pathway.

rationales.a: Prefrontal cortex supports executive functions and working memory, but the source links this memory-consolidation pathway to mammillary structures.
rationales.b: Neocortex stores long-term representations but is not the specific suprasellar lesion target described.
rationales.d: Amygdala is important for emotional learning, not the mammillary/hippocampal consolidation route asked here.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q014.takeaway: Desensitization is not the synaptic-plasticity mechanism listed in this learning framework.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q014.displayText: Synaptic plasticity and learning include post-tetanic potentiation, habituation, sensitization, long-term potentiation (LTP), and long-term depression (LTD). Desensitization is not the learning mechanism in this list. PTP lasts up to about a minute; LTP is a persistent postsynaptic enhancement, classically studied in hippocampus; LTD weakens synapses.

rationales.a: Post-tetanic potentiation is an enhanced postsynaptic response after a brief high-frequency train and is a plasticity mechanism.
rationales.b: Habituation is nonassociative learning from repeated neutral stimulation.
rationales.d: LTP is persistent enhancement after repeated presynaptic stimulation and is a core plasticity mechanism.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q015.displayText: Long-term potentiation is a persistent increase in postsynaptic response after repeated high-frequency presynaptic stimulation. It is classically observed in hippocampal circuits and depends on NMDA-receptor mechanisms, providing a cellular model for learning and memory.

rationales.c: Long-term depression decreases synaptic strength and is the opposite direction from the potentiation asked about.
rationales.d: Habituation is behavioral nonassociative learning, not the hippocampal synaptic potentiation phenomenon.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q016.takeaway: Wernicke’s area is in posterior superior temporal gyrus.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q016.displayText: Wernicke’s language-comprehension region lies in posterior superior temporal gyrus, behind primary auditory cortex. It supports comprehension; Broca’s area in inferior frontal gyrus organizes motor speech and word formation.

rationales.b: Precentral gyrus contains primary motor cortex, not Wernicke’s language-comprehension region.
rationales.c: Postcentral gyrus is primary somatosensory cortex; Wernicke’s region lies in posterior superior temporal cortex.
rationales.d: Inferior frontal gyrus contains Broca’s motor-speech area, not Wernicke’s area.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q017.displayText: Broca’s aphasia is nonfluent and effortful, with impaired word formation and repetition; comprehension is relatively preserved. It follows a lesion in inferior frontal motor-speech cortex. Aphasia reflects language dysfunction rather than primary hearing, vision, or motor paralysis.

rationales.b: Fluency is impaired in Broca’s aphasia, making this statement true.
rationales.c: The source describes speech as impoverished and nonfluent, without the fluent neologisms typical of some posterior aphasias.

marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q018.takeaway: Broca-area injury impairs word formation and speech production.
marrow__PHYS_CH18_Q018.displayText: Broca’s area in inferior frontal lobe transforms Wernicke-area language representations into coordinated motor plans for vocalization. Output passes through speech-articulation circuitry in the insula to motor cortex controlling lips, tongue, and larynx; damage therefore impairs word formation while comprehension is relatively spared.

rationales.b: Word comprehension depends more on Wernicke’s posterior temporal region than Broca’s motor-speech area.
rationales.c: Word memorization is not the primary Broca function; Broca organizes production of speech.
rationales.d: Reading relies on visual and language networks, while the specific Broca deficit is motor word formation.
